newsitem.title: USA: New trial set in Houston cancer doctor's case.
newsitem.headline: New trial set in Houston cancer doctor's case.

text.p: A federal judge on Monday declared a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a verdict in the trial of a Houston doctor charged with illegally dispensing an experimental cancer drug to patients.

After seven days of deliberations, the 12-member jury said it was evenly divided over whether physician Stanislaw Burzynski was guilty of violating federal drug laws by dispensing antineoplaston, an experimental drug derived from peptides in human urine and blood.

After the jury said it was deadlocked, U.S. District Court Judge Simeon Lake dismissed mail fraud allegations against Burzynski and his clinic, and scheduled a new trial to start on May 19 on the remaining fraud and contempt charges.

"It is more important for (the patients) than for me because my life was not really at stake but their life is at stake," Burzynski said in declaring victory in his latest battle with the government over the experimental treatment.

Burzynski, 54, was charged in a 75-count indictment with criminal contempt and fraud for allegedly violating earlier federal court orders by dispensing the experimental drug to patients across the country for ailments ranging from AIDS and cancer to skin diseases and baldness, prosecutors said.

The case attracted national attention as Burzynski's cancer patients picketed the courthouse protesting that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's lengthy drug review process was robbing them of their last hope for a cure.
Although they were told the effectiveness of the drug was not an issue in the case, half of the jurors said they had Burzynski's cancer patients in mind during deliberations.

"On a personal level, if people have no other alternative and they want to try an experimental treatment, they should be able to," juror Sharon Wray, 37, said, calling the prosecution's case a "government witch hunt."

Court orders issued in 1983 and 1984 prohibited Burzynski from dispensing the drug to Texas patients. Prosecutors said he got around the prohibition by having patients, many critically ill, come to Texas to receive the drug.

Burzynski has dispensed antineoplaston manufactured at his Houston plant to more than 2,500 patients over the past 13 years, pulling in $40 million from patients and insurance companies, prosecutors said.

Burzynski has since filed a new drug application with the FDA and is treating about 300 patients legally in clinical trials as he collects data on the effectiveness of the antineoplaston treatment, he said.
"Now the ball's in the FDA's court. Let's see what they do. They should approve this drug and stop the insanity," defense attorney Rick Jaffe said.
